name: Serpent Crown
geological_features: A ring system of extraordinary density composed of ice and silicate fragments
Banded atmospheric layers with serpentine wind patterns visible from orbit
A metallic hydrogen core generating an intense magnetic field
specific_features: Ring fragments that appear to be artificially sorted by size and composition in discrete bands
resources: Ice and silicate materials from the ring system
Fusion fuel from the hydrogen-rich upper atmosphere
description: Serpent Crown is a gas giant crowned by one of the most spectacular ring systems ever cataloged. The rings extend in dense, sharply defined bands for nearly two hundred thousand kilometers from the planet's equator, their ice and silicate fragments catching starlight in a display that has been visible to civilizations on neighboring worlds throughout their history. The planet itself is a roiling mass of hydrogen and helium, its atmospheric bands writhing in sinuous patterns that give the impression of enormous serpents coiling beneath the cloud tops.

The magnetic field generated by Serpent Crown's metallic hydrogen core is fierce enough to disrupt electronics on unshielded vessels at considerable distance. Auroral displays at the poles are visible in wavelengths from radio to ultraviolet, creating curtains of light hundreds of kilometers tall. The ring system casts complex shadow patterns on the cloud tops, and during the planet's long solstice, the shadow of the rings creates a dark band across the equator that makes the serpentine wind patterns stand out in sharp relief.

The ring system's most puzzling feature is its organization. Natural ring systems are typically mixed, their materials distributed by orbital mechanics without regard for composition. Serpent Crown's rings are sorted, each band containing fragments of uniform size and chemical makeup, as though sieved by an intelligence with patience measured in geological time. No mechanism for this sorting has been proposed that does not invoke deliberate action, yet no other evidence of agency has been found.

Atmospheric harvesting operations maintain a careful distance from the planet, using the ring system's outer edge as a navigation reference. The helium-3 yields are excellent, but the magnetic field makes close approach hazardous and expensive. The sorted rings remain a topic of vigorous academic debate, with proposals ranging from resonance effects with unknown moons to the remnants of a megastructure that once encircled the planet. The fragments themselves, when sampled, show no signs of manufacture.
